source.title: How BPE Affects Memorization in Transformers
source.authors: E. Kharitonov; M. Baroni; Dieuwke Hupkes

record.tranche_reason: Tests random-label memorization with Transformer NLP models while varying BPE vocabulary size, rather than reproducing the original image-classification setup. Also measures related memorization outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study varies tokenization granularity and measures random-label training accuracy. Membership-inference, recovery, and sequence-length results bear on memorization but not on the listed versions unless they measure the behavior named there. Figure-only trends are described qualitatively in text; no numeric values were reconstructed from plots. Appendix E reports membership-inference results on machine translation but those do not measure any listed version.
record.test_reason: The study measures training accuracy on independently randomized labels in a new setting: Transformer classifiers on text and binary strings. These results test V1's fitting behavior, although chance test performance and unchanged true-label training settings are not established.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: larger BPE vocabularies improve random-mapping fitting, membership-inference vulnerability and training-data recovery, including with approximately controlled parameter counts. Shorter sequences are the authors' proposed explanation, supported by exclusion of alternatives rather than conclusively isolated as the sole cause.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Transformer NLP models and BPE vocabulary sweeps to study random mappings, membership inference, and training-data recovery; does not reproduce image classification or hold architecture and optimizer fixed while changing true labels to random labels.
record.method_sensitivity: BPE vocabulary size changes training accuracy; parameter control preserves the trend. The study also reports effects for model architecture and attention-head count.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger BPE vocabularies increase membership-inference AUC on true-label SNLI; hold-out accuracy remains above 0.78 and sometimes also improves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokenization can affect membership-inference vulnerability and generalization together.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger BPE vocabularies improve prompted recovery of PAQ training answers, and larger models outperform smaller ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vocabulary and model size affect recovery of factual training content.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger BPE vocabularies increase membership-inference vulnerability in English-Dutch translation models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tokenization affects membership-inference vulnerability in Transformer sequence-to-sequence models.

record.problems: Results in Figures 1–8 are supplied mostly as plots without exact values; random-label SNLI results use a modified classifier setup, including a 1-layer Encoder after preliminary runs; results are from NLP datasets rather than image classification. Three random seeds are reported for the random-label SNLI experiments. Membership inference and recovery probe different memorization facets.

untested.parts: Chance test error on randomized labels and fitting without changing architecture or training hyperparameters relative to true-label training are not established. The random-label experiment disables dropout, allows 500 epochs, and substitutes a shallower Encoder to expose vocabulary effects.
No matched true-label versus random-label fitting-time comparison or corruption-fraction convergence sweep.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments. Binary strings do not test these named input transformations.
No corruption-fraction sweep jointly measuring training fit and test degradation.
No comparison establishing whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
No training trajectories comparing acquisition of shared real-data patterns with subsequent memorization of noise.

missing.what: Preliminary four-layer Encoder reaches 100% random-label training accuracy irrespective of vocabulary size. This directly supports V1 and explains the deliberate switch to a one-layer Encoder.

Random-label fitting on binary strings under an idealized tokenization procedure with uniformly distributed tokens: vocabularies of 2, 4, 16 and 256, with sequence length halved at each step. The text reports improved fitting despite fixed uniform token frequencies; absolute model-specific accuracies require the figure.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was used. Missing numerical plot values do not themselves justify limits_scope verdicts. R22 and R23 measure the behavior named by V1 even though they investigate its mechanisms. Random-label assignment is the defining experimental manipulation for V1, rather than a reason to exclude these experiments.

versions.untested_parts: Tests random mappings on SNLI and artificial random sequences with Transformers; does not test random image labels, test error at chance, or the original architectures and hyperparameters.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or of convergence time as corruption fraction changes.
Does not test shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise image inputs.
Does not sweep corrupted-label fractions while measuring both perfect training fit and test error.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal in the context of random labels and true-label generalization.
Does not compare learning of shared real-data patterns with later memorization of noise over training.

rows.subject: Encoder

rows.value: around 87%
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 shaded area ±1 SEM; exact value not stated
rows.note: Reported explicitly in text for the smallest vocabulary. Not zero or near-zero training error.
rows.check: Around 87% training accuracy demonstrates substantial but incomplete fitting after the training budget.

rows.subject: Encoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained to fit equiprobable random binary labels on filtered SNLI examples; vocabulary varied by BPE; 3 random seeds per vocabulary size.
rows.value: more than 98%
rows.uncertainty: Figure 1 shaded area ±1 SEM; exact uncertainty not stated
rows.note: Reported explicitly in text. The study's early stopping criterion was training accuracy at least 0.999, but this result is reported as more than 98%.
rows.check: More than 98% training accuracy means less than 2% training error, reasonably qualifying as near-zero. The record incorrectly treats failure to establish exactly zero error as failure of V1.
